title: Left Hop Converter
context: Grade 5, the pages on converting smaller units into bigger ones. An adult sees decimal points moving. What the pages are doing is making a conversion a matter of counting places between two units, where each place to the left divides the number by 10.

writeup.why: Change a measure from a smaller unit to a bigger one by counting the places from the unit you have to the unit you want and dividing the number by 10 for each, write a mixed measure as one decimal, split a measure into two units, and name the unit of every decimal.
writeup.look: One row of the unit chart with digit tiles in its columns, two pins for the unit you have and the unit you want, and a point that hops left.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Left Hop Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of hops the point has made. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. One row of the chart runs across the middle of the area at y 380: seven columns, each 140 wide, from x 90 to x 1070, headed kilo to milli with the base unit in the middle and the unit names violet, labelled Unit. The given measure stands in deep blue digit tiles, labelled Given, one to a column, with the point in the gap after its unit. The deep blue have pin stands over the unit you have at y 300, and the green want pin is dragged along the same line to the unit you want. The Hop button stands at x 900, y 230. Each hop moves the point one gap to the left and draws a vermilion arrow under the row along y 470, labelled Move, divide the number by 10. A grey zero, labelled Place holder, drops into any column between the point and the digits that would otherwise stand empty. The Cut handle is a short upright bar that slides along the gaps of the row. The unit tags wait in a tray at x 120, y 560, and the answer is read in green, labelled Answer, at x 120, y 660, only once a tag is clipped to it. The unit in use is amber. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key and a delete key. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. The measure the question gives, in the unit it is given in, is deep blue, labelled Given or Measure. The measure the working reaches, and a reading on a scale, is green, labelled Answer, Reading or Same measure. The places moved across the unit chart, and the worth of one small mark on a scale, are vermilion, labelled Move or One mark. A unit fact, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet, labelled Unit fact, Unit or Other scale. The part taken away, and a part left over after sharing, are rose, labelled Taken away or Left over. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open inside a number, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. Rulers, tapes, jugs, scales, thermometer tubes, chart lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last measure stays on the row with its hops drawn beneath, its point after the unit wanted and its unit tag clipped on.

phases.win: the point stops after the metres digit, and the two hops glow vermilion beneath
phases.does: drags the want pin to m, counts the places between the pins, and hops the point once for each
phases.goal: count the places from the unit you have to the unit you want; each place to the left divides the number by 10
phases.says: Pin the unit you want. How many places away is it?
phases.check: Away from the screen: from millimetres to centimetres, which way do you go, and how many places?
phases.feels: the point sliding left and the number shrinking while the length stays the same
phases.hands: Draw the chart's seven columns on paper and write a length in centimetres, one digit to a column. Put a coin on centimetres and another on metres, count the steps between them, and move a paper point one column left for each.
phases.tries: First rung: pin the unit you want and count the places without hopping. Second rung: hop once and read the measure. Third rung: the same task between two neighbouring units, one place apart, before the question's own measure returns.

wrong.why: counting on fingers touches every column, not every step

writeup.delight: On the third phase, when the Cut handle drops into the right gap, the row splits in two and the metres half and the centimetres half slide apart into two green cards, each with its own unit tag already clipped on.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet hopped. On the first phase a length in centimetres sits in the row, one digit to a column, with the have pin on centimetres and the want pin lying loose above. On the second a weight's two parts sit in their own columns with one place empty between them. On the third a length in centimetres sits in the row with the Cut handle resting beside the metres column. On the fourth a capacity's decimal is built with a tray of unit tags beside it. One thing moves, once: the want pin, the point, the Cut handle or the tag tray gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any measure set on any row, pinned and hopped left to any bigger unit, cut into two units, and tagged. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on counting places, mixed measures as one decimal, splitting into two units, and naming the unit of a decimal.
voiceLines: A measure on the chart, and a pin on its unit.
Pin the unit you want. How many places away is it?
Where does the point go? Is any place empty?
Cut it where the metres end. What is left in centimetres?
Which unit is this decimal in? Clip it on.
A new measure. Pin the unit you want.
Free play. Set any measure and hop it anywhere to the left.
Look at the two pins. How many places apart are they?
You hopped left to a bigger unit, and named it.

observations.why: a bigger unit needs fewer of itself to make the same length.
observations.soWhat: moving to a bigger unit divides the number, never the thing measured.
observations.observe: Each hop to the left made the number smaller, but the length on the card stayed the same.

observations.why: each unit is 10 times the unit to its right, so each place is one divide by 10.
observations.soWhat: count the places from the unit you have to the unit you want before hopping.
observations.observe: The number of hops was the number of places between the two pins.

observations.why: each place after the point is one unit of the chart, and an empty one must be held open.
observations.soWhat: the zero keeps every digit in its own unit's column.
observations.observe: A grey zero dropped in wherever a place after the point had no digit.

observations.why: the unit decides what each digit is worth.
observations.soWhat: a decimal is only a measure once its unit is written with it.
observations.observe: The same digits read with another tag named a very different measure.

description: Pin the unit you have and the unit you want, hop the measure left one place at a time, and watch the number divided by 10 at each hop, then clip the unit onto the decimal.

source_tool.description: One row of the unit chart runs across the working area, seven columns from kilo to milli with the base unit in the middle and the unit names in violet, labelled Unit. The measure the question gives is set in deep blue digit tiles, labelled Given, one digit to a column, with the point after its unit. A deep blue pin stands on the unit you have and a green pin is dragged to the unit you want. The Hop button moves the point one column to the left; each hop draws a vermilion arrow under the row, labelled Move, divide the number by 10, and the running count at the top left of the canvas counts the hops. Where a place between the point and the digits would be empty, a grey zero drops in, labelled Place holder. On the second phase a mixed measure drops in as its two parts, each in its own unit's columns. On the third a Cut handle splits the measure at a unit's column into two units. The answer is read in green, labelled Answer, only after a unit tag has been clipped to it; the unit in use is amber.
source_tool.art_direction: Hopping counters along a chalk chart / Picture book

The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a unit chart of seven columns from kilo to milli with the base unit in the middle, rulers and tapes marked in their units, kitchen scales, measuring jugs marked in millilitres, and thermometers with labelled marks.
Every measure is written with its unit on every line, and every decimal names the unit it is in, so 3.04 L is never shown as a bare 3.04.
Every mixed measure shown is ordinary: its smaller part is less than one of the larger unit.
Places are counted from the unit the child has to the unit the child wants, one hop at a time, and each hop shows the number, not the unit, divided or multiplied by 10.
Multiplying and dividing a measure happen in its smallest unit, in whole numbers, and a sharing that does not come out even shows what is left over.
A thermometer shows what one small mark is worth before its column is read, and a Celsius reading sits beside a Fahrenheit one only in the four pairs the chapter prints.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a hop across the chart, a carry across units, a length shared into equal pieces, or a column rising to a mark.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a unit or a mark the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the measure the question gives is deep blue, and the measure the working reaches, with a reading taken off a scale, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The places moved across the unit chart, each one dividing or multiplying the number by 10, and the worth of one small mark on a scale are vermilion. A unit fact such as 1 kg = 1000 g, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet. The part taken away, and a remainder left over after sharing, are rose. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Move, Unit fact, Taken away, Left over and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the two pins. How many places apart are they?
voice.onNext: A new measure. Pin the unit you want.
voice.opening: A measure on the chart, and a pin on its unit.
voice.onFinish: You hopped left to a bigger unit, and named it.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Set any measure and hop it anywhere to the left.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A mixed measure as one decimal

placement.where: After the class has measured ribbons in centimetres and written each length again in metres by counting places on their floor chart. The tool is what hops the point one place at a time and drops the zeros in, which paper can only show finished.

answer_key.rule: Count the places from the unit you have to the unit you want. Each place to the left divides the number by 10, so one place divides by 10, two by 100 and three by 1000. A mixed measure is written as one decimal in the larger unit, with a zero holding any empty place after the point. A measure can be split into two units at a unit's column. Every decimal is written with the unit it is in.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the child's point where they put it and reads the measure back in that form, with the unit they named. Beside it the pins light amber, and the places between them are counted again one hop at a time in vermilion. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Count the places from the unit you have to the unit you want: from cm to m is two places to the left.
Each place to the left divides the number by 10, so divide by 10 twice, which is dividing by 100.
items.question: A garden hose is 1285 cm long. How long is it in metres?
items.checkpoint: Count the places from the unit you have to the unit you want, and divide the number by 10 for each place to the left.
items.misconception: Multiplying by 100 instead of dividing, because the two places were counted but not their direction; the hose would come out longer than a whole town.

steps: 1000 g make 1 kg, so 36 g is 36 thousandths of a kilogram.
36 thousandths is written 0.036, with a zero holding the tenths place open.
Put the 8 kilograms in front of the point.
items.question: Write 8 kg 36 g in kilograms.
items.checkpoint: A mixed measure is one decimal in the larger unit, with a zero holding any empty place after the point.
items.misconception: Leaving out the zero and writing 8.36 kg, which is 8 kg 360 g, a much heavier load.

steps: Split the measure at the metres: 915 cm is 900 cm + 15 cm.
900 divided by 100 is 9, so 900 cm is 9 m.
items.question: A rope is 915 cm long. Write its length in metres and centimetres.
items.checkpoint: Split a measure at a unit's column to write it in two units.
items.misconception: Dividing by 10 instead of by 100, which gives 91 m 5 cm, far longer than the rope.

steps: 1000 mL make 1 litre, so 65 mL is 65 thousandths of a litre.
Written after the point, 65 thousandths is 0.065.
Clip the unit on: the digits alone do not say whether they mean litres or millilitres.
items.answer: 1.065 L. The unit says the decimal is in litres; read in millilitres, the same digits would be about one drop.
items.question: A flask holds 1 L 65 mL. Write it as a decimal in litres, and say why the unit must be written.
items.checkpoint: Every decimal is written with the unit it is in.
items.misconception: Writing 1.65 L, as if 65 mL were 65 hundredths of a litre, which puts 650 mL in the flask.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: From mL to L on the chart, how many places is it, and which way?
Write 37 dm in metres and decimetres.
Write 3 kg 7 g as a decimal in kilograms, and name the unit.
Are 4.3 kg and 4.3 g the same weight?
items.final_answer: No. 4.3 kg is 4300 g, but 4.3 g is a small pinch. The unit tells which

items.question: Write 2064 g in kilograms and grams.
Write 7 kL 45 L as a decimal in kilolitres.

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Count the places from the unit you have to the unit you want, wherever those two units sit on the chart, and not from the middle of the chart. It is the number that is divided by 10 for each place to the left. Say the unit aloud with every decimal, and accept any correct form when a question does not name the unit. The zeros after the point hold empty places open: 36 g is 0.036 kg, not 0.36 kg.

A deep blue pin marks the unit you have and a green pin is dragged to the unit you want. A Hop button moves the point one column left and draws a vermilion arrow labelled Move, divide the number by 10; a grey zero drops into any place that would be empty. The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Pin the unit you have and the unit you want. Hop left once for each place, and divide the number by 10 each time. Clip the unit onto the decimal.
